notes: Materialize input.files beneath a fresh directory, then input.symlinks; call packDirectory with input.entrypoint. Always remove temporary directories.
contentBase64 encodes exact bytes. Symlink target is relative to the link; targetType directory is only a filesystem setup hint. Symlinks must be rejected even if safe-looking or dangling.

Ordering: packDirectory places file entries in manifest.files by sorting the COMPLETE artifact path strings lexicographically by Unicode code-point values (numerically at the first difference; a shorter prefix first), exactly the relation canonical JSON uses for object keys. No locale collation, no Unicode normalization, no case folding, no natural/numeric ordering, no UTF-16 code-unit ordering; the exact strings the filesystem exposed are compared. pack-unicode-code-point-order and pack-unicode-no-normalization are the portable Unicode anchors (U+E000 sorts before U+10000). Canonicalization itself still preserves any existing files array order; manually authored manifests are not required to be sorted.
expected.manifest, canonicalJson, artifactDigest, blobDigests are static independent goldens; every returned blob must also equal the source bytes.

pack-cross-language-anchor is the static rendezvous point for independent implementations (issue #31): the JavaScript reference and the Go conformance implementation each check its expected canonicalJson, artifactDigest and blobDigests from this file; neither calls the other. Four entries share one content digest under two media types and the names span ASCII, Greek, CJK, private-use and supplementary code points.

Media types (issue #33): packDirectory assigns file.mediaType from the complete artifact path alone, by the fixed table and extension rule in spec-v0.2.md (Directory packing, Media type assignment): take the final path segment; the extension is the suffix from its FINAL '.'; there is no extension when the segment has no '.' or when that '.' is its first character (dotfiles such as .env and .html); fold ASCII A-Z to a-z in the lookup key only; everything unlisted is application/octet-stream. No host MIME database, no byte inspection, no compound extensions (archive.tar.gz uses only .gz); the path itself is never altered. pack-media-type-table pins every table entry; pack-media-type-uppercase-extensions, pack-media-type-fallback, pack-media-type-multiple-dots and pack-media-type-no-byte-sniffing pin the edge behaviour. This is producer behaviour: manually authored manifests may carry any nonempty mediaType.

A name ending in '.' has the extension '.' and is therefore application/octet-stream; that case is pinned by direct implementation tests in both runners rather than by a materialized vector, because Win32 removes a trailing dot from file names and such a fixture would not materialize identically on every platform.

Portable Unicode filenames (safe on Linux, macOS and Windows; no case-only pairs; no canonically-equivalent pairs) in deliberately scrambled fixture order. packDirectory must order COMPLETE artifact paths by Unicode code points: "." (U+002E) sorts before "/" (U+002F) so /a.txt precedes /a/x.txt; ASCII < Greek (U+03A9) < CJK (U+4E2D) < private-use U+E000 < supplementary U+10000 < U+1F331. U+E000 before U+10000 is the code-point-versus-UTF-16 anchor: a UTF-16 code-unit sort would put U+10000 (lead surrogate U+D800) first.

Filenames that look alike but are distinct code-point sequences and are NOT canonically equivalent (so they coexist on Linux, macOS and Windows): ASCII digits/letters versus superscript two (U+00B2), circled digit one (U+2460) and fullwidth f (U+FF46), plus 10 versus 9 versus 2; no name has a Unicode case folding onto another (so case-insensitive filesystems keep them apart). packDirectory must compare the exact strings by code point: no Unicode normalization (compatibility folding would merge them), no case folding, no natural/numeric ordering ("10" sorts before "2" and "9").

Static cross-implementation anchor (issue #31): seven files in scrambled fixture order whose complete artifact paths must sort by Unicode code point (ASCII < Greek U+03A9 < CJK U+4E2D < private-use U+E000 < supplementary U+1F331, and /assets/<U+10000>.js first because "a" < "i"), while four entries — three .txt and one .js under three different directories — hold identical bytes and therefore share ONE content digest under TWO different OWA media types. The expected canonical JSON, artifact digest and blob digests were authored with an independent standard-library encoder; every conforming implementation, in any language, must reproduce them from this input without consulting another implementation.
Every extension of the fixed pack media-type table (issue #33), lowercase, one file each in scrambled fixture order; the table is closed, nothing else is mapped.

Known extensions match after folding ASCII A-Z to a-z in the lookup key only: INDEX.HTML, App.MJS, IMAGE.PNG, Data.Json, README.TXT and Theme.CsS map exactly as their lowercase forms while every artifact path keeps its exact case and sorts by code point (uppercase before lowercase). No case-only name pairs, so the fixture materializes on case-insensitive filesystems.

application/octet-stream for a name without a dot (README), a dotfile whose only dot is its first character even when the name resembles a known extension (.env, .html), an unlisted extension (file.xyz), an unlisted FINAL extension after several dots (archive.json.gz: no compound-extension rule, only .gz is examined), and a file without an extension inside a directory whose name has one (vendor.json/LICENSE: only the final path segment is examined).

Only the suffix from the FINAL dot is the extension: archive.tar.JSON is .json (folded), jquery.min.js is .js, theme.dark.css is .css, chart.svg.PNG is .png (an earlier known-looking part is irrelevant), .hidden.html is .html (a dotfile WITH a later dot has an extension) and foo..txt is .txt (consecutive dots are ordinary characters).

The media type comes from the artifact path alone; file bytes are never inspected: index.html holding a PNG signature is still text/html, logo.png holding SVG text is still image/png, lib.wasm holding JSON is still application/wasm, notes.txt holding arbitrary binary is still text/plain, and README holding HTML is still application/octet-stream.
